library(nlmixr2lib)

# Model and source

* Citation: Tapani S, Almquist J, Leander J, Ahlstrom C, Peletier LA,
  Jirstrand M, Gabrielsson J. Joint feedback analysis modeling of
  nonesterified fatty acids in obese Zucker rats and normal Sprague-Dawley
  rats after different routes of administration of nicotinic acid.
  *J Pharm Sci* 2014;103(8):2571-2584.
* Article (open access): [doi:10.1002/jps.24077](https://doi.org/10.1002/jps.24077)

The paper fits a pharmacodynamic feedback model of plasma non-esterified fatty
acids (NEFA) after nicotinic acid (NiAc) dosing to pooled data from normal
Sprague-Dawley and obese Zucker rats. Its main result is a **joint** model in
which three NEFA parameters (baseline `R0`, fractional turnover `kout` and the
sigmoidicity `gamma`) differ between the strains and the rest are shared. As a
comparator, the authors refit the same model **separately** to each strain.
The library ships all three parameter sets:

| Model | Content |
|-------|---------|
| `Tapani_2014_nicotinicAcid_rat` | Joint model (Table 4 "Joint Analysis"); the strain is selected by `DIS_OBESE` |
| `Tapani_2014_nicotinicAcid_rat_normal` | Separate fit to the Sprague-Dawley rats (Table 4 "Separate Analysis") |
| `Tapani_2014_nicotinicAcid_rat_obese` | Separate fit to the obese Zucker rats (Table 4 "Separate Analysis") |

The NiAc pharmacokinetics were not re-estimated. Table 1 prints the earlier
published estimates, and all three models fix them. Normal rats have a
two-compartment model with two parallel Michaelis-Menten eliminations,
endogenous synthesis and parallel linear plus saturable gut absorption (Eqs. 1-3).
Obese rats have a one-compartment model with one Michaelis-Menten
elimination and endogenous synthesis (Eq. 4).

The NEFA model is the feedback model of Ahlstrom et al. (see also
`Ahlstrom_2010_nicotinicAcid_rat` in this library). NiAc inhibits NEFA
formation through `I(Cp) = 1 - Imax Cp^gamma / (IC50^gamma + Cp^gamma)`.
A chain of eight moderator compartments, all turning over at `ktol`, provides
the feedback: the first moderator divides the formation rate (raised to the
power `p`), and the eighth multiplies the loss rate. `kcap` is a NiAc-independent
formation term (Eqs. 5-10):

```
dR/dt   = kin I(Cp) / M1^p + kcap - kout R M8
dM1/dt  = ktol (R - M1),   dMi/dt = ktol (M(i-1) - Mi),  i = 2..8
kin     = (kout R0^2 - kcap) R0^p
```

```{r models}
mod_joint <- readModelDb("Tapani_2014_nicotinicAcid_rat")
mod_norm <- readModelDb("Tapani_2014_nicotinicAcid_rat_normal")
mod_obese <- readModelDb("Tapani_2014_nicotinicAcid_rat_obese")
```

# Population

The data were pooled from earlier NiAc/NEFA studies at AstraZeneca R&D
Molndal. All animals were male, 16 weeks old at the experiment, and fasted
14 h before dosing and throughout the experiment.

- **Sprague-Dawley rats** (220-367 g) received IV infusions of vehicle, 1, 5
  or 20 umol/kg over 30 min, or vehicle, 5, 10 or 51 umol/kg over 300 min.
  Other groups received oral gavage of vehicle or 24.4, 81.2 or 812 umol/kg,
  or a 5 umol/kg 30-min infusion followed by stepwise-decreasing infusion
  rates, with or without a second 30-min infusion at 210 min.
- **Obese Zucker (fa/fa) rats** (473-547 g) received vehicle or 20 umol/kg
  IV over 30 min, or vehicle or 51 umol/kg IV over 300 min.

The printed group sizes add up to about 99 Sprague-Dawley and 19 obese rats.
There were 1440 NEFA observations. The same information is available
programmatically via `readModelDb("Tapani_2014_nicotinicAcid_rat")()$population`.

# Source trace

Every `ini()` value carries an in-file comment that points to its table cell.

| Quantity | Joint (normal / obese) | Separate normal | Separate obese | Source |
|----------|------------------------|-----------------|----------------|--------|
| `R0` (mmol/L) | 0.741 / 1.07 | 0.739 | 1.04 | Table 4 |
| `kout` (L/mmol/min) | 0.290 / 0.343 | 0.316 | 0.0683 | Table 4 |
| `ktol` (1/min) | 0.0245 | 0.0239 | 0.0697 | Table 4 |
| `kcap` (mmol/L/min) | 0.0245 | 0.0281 | 4.94e-8 | Table 4 |
| `p` | 1.20 | 1.15 | 3.19 | Table 4 |
| `IC50` (umol/L) | 0.0820 | 0.0757 | 0.0433 | Table 4 |
| `gamma` | 2.16 / 0.298 | 2.19 | 0.563 | Table 4 |
| `Imax` | 1 (fixed) | 1 (fixed) | 1 (fixed) | Table 4, Initial Parameter Estimates |
| IIV `R0` (%) | 19.7 / 24.0 | 19.9 | 15.8 | Table 4 |
| IIV `kout` (%) | 71.4 / 151 | 47.4 | 29.7 | Table 4 |
| IIV `IC50` (%) | 129 | 134 | 74.7 | Table 4 |
| NEFA residual `sigma2` | 0.0110 | 0.0102 | 0.0111 | Table 4 |
| NiAc PK (Vmax1, Km1, Vmax2, Km2, Vc, Vt, Cld, Synt, ka, Vmax,g, Km,g; IIV; sigma1) | normal / obese columns | normal column | obese column | Table 1 |
| Gut absorption | Eq. 1 | Eq. 1 | n/a | Methods |
| NiAc disposition | Eqs. 2-4 | Eqs. 2-3 | Eq. 4 | Methods |
| NEFA, moderators, `I(Cp)`, `kin` | Eqs. 5-10 | Eqs. 5-10 | Eqs. 5-10 | Methods |
| Strain switch | Eq. 11 (`Z = 1 - DIS_OBESE`) | n/a | n/a | Methods |

The derived `kin` values match the secondary parameters that Table 4 prints:

```{r kin-check}
kin_of <- function(r0, kout, kcap, p) (kout * r0^2 - kcap) * r0^p
kin_tab <- data.frame(
  model = c("joint normal", "joint obese", "separate normal", "separate obese"),
  kin_model = c(
    kin_of(0.741, 0.290, 0.0245, 1.20), kin_of(1.07, 0.343, 0.0245, 1.20),
    kin_of(0.739, 0.316, 0.0281, 1.15), kin_of(1.04, 0.0683, 4.94e-8, 3.19)
  ),
  kin_table4 = c(0.0940, 0.399, 0.102, 0.0837)
)
kin_tab$pct_diff <- 100 * (kin_tab$kin_model / kin_tab$kin_table4 - 1)
knitr::kable(kin_tab, digits = c(0, 4, 4, 2))
# Deterministic: only the rounding of the printed inputs separates the columns.
stopifnot(all(abs(kin_tab$pct_diff) < 1))
```

# Simulation helpers

The models are written per kilogram of body weight. Doses are in umol/kg,
NiAc concentrations in umol/L and NEFA in mmol/L, with time in minutes. IV
infusions dose `central` and oral doses dose `depot`. Both endpoints (`Cc` and
`NEFA`) are returned by observing on `central` with `dvid = 1`.

```{r helpers}
obs_times <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 60, by = 1), seq(62, 600, by = 2))))

# One event table per subject block. `dose` umol/kg over `dur` min (IV), or an
# oral bolus when `route = "oral"`.
make_events <- function(n, dose, dur, route = "iv", times = obs_times,
                        id_offset = 0L, DIS_OBESE = NULL) {
  ids <- id_offset + seq_len(n)
  dosing <- data.frame(
    id = ids, time = 0, evid = 1L, amt = dose,
    rate = if (route == "iv") dose / dur else 0,
    cmt = if (route == "iv") "central" else "depot", dvid = NA_integer_
  )
  obs <- expand.grid(id = ids, time = times)
  obs <- data.frame(
    id = obs$id, time = obs$time, evid = 0L, amt = 0, rate = 0,
    cmt = "central", dvid = 1L
  )
  ev <- dplyr::arrange(rbind(dosing, obs), id, time, dplyr::desc(evid))
  if (!is.null(DIS_OBESE)) ev$DIS_OBESE <- DIS_OBESE
  ev
}

solve_typical <- function(mod, ev) {
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod), ev))
}
```

# Typical NEFA profiles after a 20 umol/kg 30-min infusion (Figure 6)

Figure 6 overlays the typical-individual NEFA curves for a 20 umol/kg 30-min
infusion. Panels a and c use the separate models and panels b and d the joint
model, for normal and obese rats respectively. The points below were digitised
from the published figure at times where the curve is well separated from the
observed data.

```{r fig6}
ev20 <- make_events(1, dose = 20, dur = 30)
typ <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  solve_typical(mod_norm, ev20) |> mutate(panel = "a: separate, normal"),
  solve_typical(mod_joint, transform(ev20, DIS_OBESE = 0)) |> mutate(panel = "b: joint, normal"),
  solve_typical(mod_obese, ev20) |> mutate(panel = "c: separate, obese"),
  solve_typical(mod_joint, transform(ev20, DIS_OBESE = 1)) |> mutate(panel = "d: joint, obese")
)

fig6_digitised <- tibble::tribble(
  ~panel, ~time, ~NEFA_pub,
  "a: separate, normal", 10, 0.171, "a: separate, normal", 25, 0.128,
  "a: separate, normal", 50, 1.116, "a: separate, normal", 70, 0.848,
  "a: separate, normal", 100, 0.756, "a: separate, normal", 400, 0.756,
  "a: separate, normal", 550, 0.732,
  "b: joint, normal", 10, 0.171, "b: joint, normal", 25, 0.116,
  "b: joint, normal", 50, 1.134, "b: joint, normal", 70, 0.841,
  "b: joint, normal", 100, 0.750, "b: joint, normal", 400, 0.756,
  "b: joint, normal", 550, 0.732,
  "c: separate, obese", 20, 0.323, "c: separate, obese", 30, 0.348,
  "c: separate, obese", 55, 1.049, "c: separate, obese", 200, 0.915,
  "c: separate, obese", 400, 0.915, "c: separate, obese", 550, 0.915,
  "d: joint, obese", 10, 0.293, "d: joint, obese", 25, 0.335,
  "d: joint, obese", 60, 0.951, "d: joint, obese", 120, 0.829,
  "d: joint, obese", 300, 0.902, "d: joint, obese", 550, 0.902
)

ggplot(typ, aes(time, NEFA)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = fig6_digitised, aes(y = NEFA_pub), colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  labs(
    x = "Time (min)", y = "NEFA (mmol/L)",
    caption = "Replicates the typical curves of Figure 6 of Tapani 2014 (red: digitised)."
  )

fig6_cmp <- fig6_digitised |>
  left_join(typ |> select(panel, time, NEFA), by = c("panel", "time")) |>
  mutate(diff = NEFA - NEFA_pub)
stopifnot(nrow(fig6_cmp) == nrow(fig6_digitised), !anyNA(fig6_cmp$NEFA))
knitr::kable(fig6_cmp, digits = 3)
# Deterministic typical-value solves; the tolerance covers digitising a
# 666-pixel-wide figure (about 0.012 mmol/L per pixel) and the steep rebound
# edge, where a pixel of time is several hundredths of mmol/L.
stopifnot(max(abs(fig6_cmp$diff)) < 0.06)
```

All four typical curves match the published ones. In obese rats the curves
start at `R0` and settle at about 0.9 mmol/L, not at `R0`. The model drives
the NEFA inhibition by **total** NiAc, endogenous plus dosed. In obese rats the
endogenous NiAc steady state (about 0.033 umol/L) is close to `IC50` and,
with the shallow `gamma`, already inhibits NEFA formation by more than 40%.
The published figure shows the same settling level, which supports that the
paper's model is driven by total NiAc and starts the NEFA states at `R0`.

```{r endogenous}
# Steady state of Eq. 5 with M1 = M8 = R at a constant NiAc concentration.
# For kin > 0 the balance falls monotonically in R and has one root. A draw
# with kout * R0^2 < kcap has kin < 0. The balance then rises and falls, and
# the larger root is the one where it falls (the stable one, which is R0 when
# there is no drug). NA if no root exists.
ss_nefa <- function(cp, r0, kout, kcap, p, ic50, gam) {
  kin <- (kout * r0^2 - kcap) * r0^p
  icp <- 1 - cp^gam / (ic50^gam + cp^gam)
  f <- function(r) kin * icp / r^p + kcap - kout * r^2
  lower <- 1e-6
  if (kin < 0) {
    lower <- optimize(f, c(1e-6, 10), maximum = TRUE)$maximum
    if (f(lower) <= 0) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }
  }
  uniroot(f, c(lower, 10), tol = 1e-12)$root
}
late <- typ |> filter(time == 600)
cp_end <- setNames(late$Cc, late$panel)
ss_check <- data.frame(
  panel = names(cp_end),
  endogenous_Cp = cp_end,
  NEFA_600 = late$NEFA,
  NEFA_steady_state = c(
    ss_nefa(cp_end[[1]], 0.739, 0.316, 0.0281, 1.15, 0.0757, 2.19),
    ss_nefa(cp_end[[2]], 0.741, 0.290, 0.0245, 1.20, 0.0820, 2.16),
    ss_nefa(cp_end[[3]], 1.04, 0.0683, 4.94e-8, 3.19, 0.0433, 0.563),
    ss_nefa(cp_end[[4]], 1.07, 0.343, 0.0245, 1.20, 0.0820, 0.298)
  )
)
knitr::kable(ss_check, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
# The 600-min value is still on a slow, damped oscillation, so this checks the
# level rather than convergence.
stopifnot(max(abs(ss_check$NEFA_600 - ss_check$NEFA_steady_state)) < 0.03)
```

# Steady-state concentration-response (Figure 5)

At a constant NiAc concentration all moderators equal `R`, and the steady
state solves `kin I(Cp) / R^p + kcap = kout R^2`. Figure 5 plots that steady
state against the NiAc concentration with 90% population bands from the IIV
of `R0`, `kout` and `IC50`. The bands are computed below from 2000 parameter
draws (base-R RNG, so they are identical on every machine).

The paper reports IIV as a percentage without saying how it relates to the
variance `omega^2` of the log-normal random effect. The models read the
percentage as `100 * omega`, so `omega^2 = (IIV/100)^2`. The joint
model's normal-rat band at high NiAc concentrations decides between the two
usual readings. There `I(Cp)` is close to 0, so `R = sqrt(kcap / kout)` and
the band width depends on the `kout` IIV alone (71.4%):

```{r fig5}
conc <- c(10^seq(-3, 1.8, by = 0.2), 100)
draw_band <- function(n, r0, kout, kcap, p, ic50, gam, om_r0, om_kout, om_ic50) {
  set.seed(20140701)
  er0 <- rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(om_r0))
  ekout <- rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(om_kout))
  eic50 <- rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(om_ic50))
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(conc, function(cp) {
    r <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
      ss_nefa(cp, r0 * exp(er0[i]), kout * exp(ekout[i]), kcap, p, ic50 * exp(eic50[i]), gam)
    }, numeric(1))
    data.frame(
      conc = cp, typical = ss_nefa(cp, r0, kout, kcap, p, ic50, gam),
      lo = unname(quantile(r, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)), hi = unname(quantile(r, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)),
      pct_kin_negative = 100 * mean(kout * exp(ekout) * (r0 * exp(er0))^2 < kcap),
      pct_no_steady_state = 100 * mean(is.na(r))
    )
  }))
}
cv2 <- function(cv) cv^2
log1cv <- function(cv) log(1 + cv^2)
bands <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  draw_band(2000, 0.741, 0.290, 0.0245, 1.20, 0.0820, 2.16, cv2(0.197), cv2(0.714), cv2(1.29)) |>
    mutate(model = "Joint", strain = "normal"),
  draw_band(2000, 1.07, 0.343, 0.0245, 1.20, 0.0820, 0.298, cv2(0.240), cv2(1.51), cv2(1.29)) |>
    mutate(model = "Joint", strain = "obese"),
  draw_band(2000, 0.739, 0.316, 0.0281, 1.15, 0.0757, 2.19, cv2(0.199), cv2(0.474), cv2(1.34)) |>
    mutate(model = "Separate", strain = "normal"),
  draw_band(2000, 1.04, 0.0683, 4.94e-8, 3.19, 0.0433, 0.563, cv2(0.158), cv2(0.297), cv2(0.747)) |>
    mutate(model = "Separate", strain = "obese")
)
bands |>
  group_by(model, strain) |>
  summarise(
    pct_kin_negative = first(pct_kin_negative),
    max_pct_no_steady_state = max(pct_no_steady_state), .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

ggplot(bands, aes(conc, typical, colour = strain, fill = strain)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  labs(
    x = "NiAc concentration (umol/L)", y = "Steady-state NEFA (mmol/L)",
    caption = "Replicates Figure 5 of Tapani 2014 (typical curve and 90% IIV band)."
  )

# Joint normal band at 100 umol/L under the two readings of the IIV %.
alt <- draw_band(2000, 0.741, 0.290, 0.0245, 1.20, 0.0820, 2.16, log1cv(0.197), log1cv(0.714), log1cv(1.29))
at100 <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  bands |> filter(model == "Joint", strain == "normal", conc == 100) |>
    mutate(reading = "omega^2 = (IIV/100)^2 (used)"),
  alt |> filter(conc == 100) |> mutate(reading = "omega^2 = log(1 + (IIV/100)^2)")
) |>
  select(reading, lo, typical, hi) |>
  mutate(lo_pub = 0.161, typical_pub = 0.291, hi_pub = 0.538)
knitr::kable(at100, digits = 3)
stopifnot(nrow(at100) == 2L)
# 2000 base-R draws: the 5%/95% quantiles carry ~1% Monte Carlo error. The
# reading used must sit closer to the digitised band edges than the other one.
err <- abs(at100$lo - at100$lo_pub) + abs(at100$hi - at100$hi_pub)
stopifnot(err[1] < err[2], err[1] < 0.05)

typ_pub <- tibble::tribble(
  ~model, ~strain, ~conc, ~pub,
  "Joint", "normal", 0.001, 0.741, "Joint", "normal", 100, 0.291,
  "Joint", "obese", 0.001, 0.997, "Joint", "obese", 100, 0.577
)
typ_cmp <- typ_pub |>
  left_join(bands |> mutate(conc = signif(conc, 3)), by = c("model", "strain", "conc")) |>
  select(model, strain, conc, typical, pub)
stopifnot(nrow(typ_cmp) == 4L, !anyNA(typ_cmp$typical))
knitr::kable(typ_cmp, digits = 3)
stopifnot(max(abs(typ_cmp$typical - typ_cmp$pub)) < 0.02)
```

The typical curves and the normal-rat band edges match Figure 5. Under the
`log(1 + CV^2)` reading the high-concentration band would be visibly narrower
than the published one.

# Rebound after 300-min infusions (Figure 7)

Figure 7 summarises the extent of the NEFA rebound after a 300-min infusion of
5, 10 or 51 umol/kg. The extent is the maximum NEFA after the infusion stops,
as a percentage above baseline, over a population sample. The rows "0%" and
"100%" degree of disease are the normal and obese rats of the joint model.

Two choices behind the published figure are not stated, and both are settled
below by reproducing it:

- **Which parameters vary.** The paper fixed each animal's NiAc PK when it
  fitted the NEFA data. Sampling only the NEFA random effects (`R0`, `kout`,
  `IC50`) reproduces the normal-rat medians. Adding the NiAc PK random
  effects lowers them markedly at 10 and 51 umol/kg. The simulation
  therefore zeroes the PK random effects.
- **Which baseline.** For normal rats `R0` and the drug-free steady state
  coincide. In obese rats endogenous NiAc holds NEFA about 15% below `R0`
  (see Figure 6). Measuring the rebound against `R0` gives obese medians near
  zero, against 13-30% in the figure. Measuring it against the drug-free
  steady state reproduces the published values, so that is the definition
  compared below.

200 animals per arm are simulated.

```{r fig7}
# NEFA random effects only: the NiAc PK random effects are set to zero.
mod_pd <- mod_joint |>
  rxode2::ini(
    etalvmax_hi = 0, etalvmax_lo = 0, etalsynt = 0, etalka = 0, etaltmax_abs = 0,
    etalvmax_hi_obese = 0, etalsynt_obese = 0
  )
rxode2::rxSetSeed(2014)
rebound_times <- c(0, seq(300, 600, by = 2))
arms <- expand.grid(dose = c(5, 10, 51), DIS_OBESE = c(0, 1))
ev7 <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(arms)), function(i) {
  make_events(200,
    dose = arms$dose[i], dur = 300, times = rebound_times,
    id_offset = (i - 1L) * 200L, DIS_OBESE = arms$DIS_OBESE[i]
  ) |> mutate(dose = arms$dose[i])
}))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(ev7[ev7$evid == 0, c("id", "time")]))
# Animals drawn with kout * R0^2 < kcap have kin < 0 (see Figure 5 above).
# Under NiAc their formation term can turn the NEFA balance negative and the
# solve may fail with solver warnings; those animals are counted and left out.
sim7 <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod_pd, ev7, keep = c("dose")))
per_id <- sim7 |>
  group_by(id, dose, DIS_OBESE) |>
  summarise(
    failed = any(!is.finite(NEFA)) || any(NEFA < 0),
    kin = first(kin), rbase = first(rbase), Cp0 = first(Cp0), kout = first(kout),
    kcap = first(kcap), pmod = first(pmod), ic50 = first(ic50), gam = first(gam),
    peak = max(NEFA[time >= 300]), .groups = "drop"
  )
per_id |>
  group_by(dose, DIS_OBESE) |>
  summarise(n = n(), n_kin_negative = sum(kin < 0), n_failed = sum(failed), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable()
stopifnot(mean(per_id$failed) < 0.05)

rebound <- per_id |>
  filter(!failed) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(drug_free = ss_nefa(Cp0, rbase, kout, kcap, pmod, ic50, gam)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!is.na(drug_free)) |>
  mutate(
    extent = 100 * (peak / drug_free - 1),
    extent_vs_R0 = 100 * (peak / rbase - 1),
    degree = ifelse(DIS_OBESE == 1, "100% (obese)", "0% (normal)")
  )

ggplot(rebound, aes(extent, degree)) +
  geom_boxplot(coef = Inf) +
  facet_wrap(~dose, scales = "free_x", labeller = label_both) +
  labs(
    x = "Extent of rebound (% above drug-free baseline)", y = "Degree of disease",
    caption = "Replicates the 0% and 100% rows of Figure 7 of Tapani 2014."
  )

fig7_pub <- tibble::tribble(
  ~dose, ~DIS_OBESE, ~median_pub,
  5, 0, 12, 10, 0, 33, 51, 0, 155,
  5, 1, 13, 10, 1, 16, 51, 1, 30
)
fig7_cmp <- rebound |>
  group_by(dose, DIS_OBESE) |>
  summarise(
    median_sim = median(extent), q25 = quantile(extent, 0.25),
    q75 = quantile(extent, 0.75), median_vs_R0 = median(extent_vs_R0), .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(fig7_pub, by = c("dose", "DIS_OBESE"))
stopifnot(nrow(fig7_cmp) == 6L, !anyNA(fig7_cmp$median_pub))
knitr::kable(fig7_cmp, digits = 1)
```

```{r fig7-gate}
# Medians of a 200-animal cohort; the bound is on the centre of the
# distribution, not its tails. 10 points, or a third of the published median,
# covers cohort noise and reading the medians off a 160-pixel-high figure.
# A transcription error in R0, kout or gamma moves the 51 umol/kg medians by
# far more.
fig7_cmp <- fig7_cmp |>
  mutate(tol = pmax(10, median_pub / 3), ok = abs(median_sim - median_pub) < tol)
stopifnot(all(fig7_cmp$ok))
```

The intermediate "degrees of disease" (20-80%) are not reproduced. For those,
the paper solved both PK models side by side and weighted their solutions, and
the packaged joint model has only one PK structure (see Assumptions and
deviations).

# NiAc pharmacokinetics (PKNCA)

The NiAc PK is inherited from earlier publications and the paper reports no
NCA. The PKNCA summary below is therefore descriptive. It covers the two IV
regimens given to both strains, with 200 animals per arm from the joint model.
The pre-dose concentration is the endogenous NiAc steady state.

```{r pknca}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20142)
pk_arms <- expand.grid(regimen = c("20 umol/kg / 30 min", "51 umol/kg / 300 min"), DIS_OBESE = c(0, 1))
pk_arms$dose <- ifelse(grepl("^20", pk_arms$regimen), 20, 51)
pk_arms$dur <- ifelse(grepl("30 min$", pk_arms$regimen), 30, 300)
ev_pk <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(pk_arms)), function(i) {
  make_events(200,
    dose = pk_arms$dose[i], dur = pk_arms$dur[i],
    times = c(0, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, 290, 300, 305, 310, 320, 330, 360, 420, 480, 600),
    id_offset = (i - 1L) * 200L, DIS_OBESE = pk_arms$DIS_OBESE[i]
  ) |> mutate(treatment = paste(ifelse(pk_arms$DIS_OBESE[i] == 1, "obese", "normal"), pk_arms$regimen[i], sep = ", "))
}))
sim_pk <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod_joint, ev_pk, keep = c("treatment")))

conc_df <- sim_pk |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  select(id, time, Cc, treatment)
dose_df <- ev_pk |>
  filter(evid == 1) |>
  select(id, time, amt, treatment)
o_conc <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc_df, Cc ~ time | treatment + id)
o_dose <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
o_data <- PKNCA::PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose,
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = 600, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE)
)
o_nca <- PKNCA::pk.nca(o_data)
nca_tab <- as.data.frame(summary(o_nca))
knitr::kable(nca_tab)

baseline_cp <- sim_pk |>
  filter(time == 0) |>
  mutate(strain = ifelse(grepl("^obese", treatment), "obese", "normal")) |>
  group_by(strain) |>
  summarise(median_endogenous_Cp_nmolL = 1000 * median(Cc), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(baseline_cp, digits = 2)
```

The typical endogenous NiAc concentration follows from Table 1:
`Synt Km1 / (Vmax1 - Synt)` = 33.3 nmol/L in obese rats, and about 7.8 nmol/L
in normal rats, where two eliminations act in parallel.

# Assumptions and deviations

- **IIV scale.** Tables 1 and 4 give IIV as a percentage with no definition.
  The models use `omega^2 = (IIV/100)^2`. At 100 umol/L the joint model's
  normal-rat 90% band in Figure 5 is digitised as 0.16-0.54 mmol/L. The
  reading used gives about 0.17-0.51 mmol/L, and `log(1 + CV^2)` gives a
  narrower 0.17-0.48 mmol/L (see the Figure 5 table). The same reading is
  applied to every random effect, including the NiAc PK ones from Table 1.
- **NEFA residual error.** Table 4 lists `sigma2` (0.0110, 0.0102 and 0.0111)
  as "Residual add. error" without units. The models read it as a variance,
  so the additive SD is `sqrt(sigma2)`, about 0.10 mmol/L. The supporting
  material defines the residual term by its variance `S`, and the individual
  fits in Figure 4 scatter by about 0.1 mmol/L around their curves. That
  scatter is incompatible with an SD of 0.011 mmol/L.
- **NiAc residual error.** Table 1's `sigma1` (42.8% normal, 40.0% obese) is
  encoded as a proportional SD of 0.428 and 0.400.
- **Endogenous NiAc drives the effect.** The NiAc states start at the
  endogenous steady state of Eqs. 2-4 ("the endogenous concentration of NiAc
  was estimated according to the solution of the Eqs. 2 and 3 at steady
  state"). The NEFA and moderator states start at `R0` (the paper's
  `Mi,0 = R0`). Because `I(Cp)` acts on total NiAc, obese rats drift from `R0`
  to about 0.9 mmol/L without any dose, as the published Figure 6c/d curves
  also do. Users wanting a drug-free steady state at `R0` would have to
  change the model; it is shipped as published.
- **Joint model strain switch.** The paper's indicator `Z` (1 = normal) is
  `1 - DIS_OBESE`. As in Eq. 11, group-specific values (`R0`, `kout`, `gamma`
  and the two NiAc PK parameter sets) are combined linearly in `DIS_OBESE`.
  The `R0` and `kout` random effects have strain-specific variances because
  Table 4 prints a separate IIV for each strain.
- **NiAc PK as one structure.** The joint model carries one PK structure. It
  becomes the obese one-compartment model by switching off the low-affinity
  elimination pathway and the peripheral exchange when `DIS_OBESE = 1`. This is
  exact for `DIS_OBESE` = 0 or 1, the only values in the data. For
  intermediate "degrees of disease", Figure 7 solved the two PK models
  side by side and weighted their solutions. The packaged model does not
  reproduce that, so only the 0% and 100% rows of Figure 7 are replicated
  here.
- **Oral dosing in obese rats.** Obese rats were not dosed orally. The joint
  model applies the normal-rat absorption parameters if `depot` is dosed with
  `DIS_OBESE = 1`, which is an extrapolation.
- **Absorption IIV.** Table 1 prints the same IIV (10.8%, RSE 93.1%) for `ka`
  and `Vmax,g`. The two are encoded as independent random effects.
- **Fixed PK.** The paper fixed the NiAc PK parameters, including their IIV
  and residual error, at the earlier estimates, so they are wrapped in
  `fixed()`. The NEFA parameters are estimates from this paper.
- **Dose labels.** The oral doses are 24.4, 81.2 and 812 umol/kg in Methods
  but 24, 82.1 and 812 umol/kg in the Figure 3 and 4 captions; the Methods
  values are used in `population`.
- **Table 3 caption.** Table 3 is captioned "ratios between estimated
  parameters in the joint and separate models". Its values
  (`kout` 1.18, `gamma` 0.138, `R0` 1.443) are in fact the obese-to-normal
  ratios within the joint model, for example 0.343 / 0.290 = 1.18. They are
  not used by the models.
- **Figure 7 settings.** The paper does not say which parameters its
  Figure 7 Monte Carlo sampled, nor what "baseline" means for the extent of
  rebound. Sampling only the NEFA random effects, and measuring against each
  animal's drug-free steady state, reproduces the published medians for
  normal and obese rats; those settings are used. The medians from
  200 simulated animals per arm are compared with medians read off Figure 7,
  which used 1000 animals per arm.
- **Negative `kin`.** `kin` is derived from `R0`, `kout` and `kcap`
  (Eq. 10). With the published IIV, about 1% of normal and 3% of obese
  joint-model draws have `kout R0^2 < kcap` and so a negative `kin`. Such
  an animal still sits at `R0` without drug, but NiAc then raises its NEFA
  formation, and its NEFA solve can fail. The paper does not mention these
  animals. The vignette counts them and leaves out any that fail to solve.
